The data is the National Center for Health Statistics’ VSRR Provisional Drug Overdose Death Counts, a public-domain CSV on data.cdc.gov that needs no key, here with deaths through May 2026. This block runs on its own (R 4.6.1, dplyr 1.2.1):
```  
library(tidyverse)

vsrr <- read_csv("https://data.cdc.gov/api/views/xkb8-kh2a/rows.csv?accessType=DOWNLOAD",  
                 show_col_types = FALSE)

od <- vsrr |>  
  filter(Indicator == "Number of Drug Overdose Deaths", State != "PR") |>  
  mutate(date   = ymd(paste(Year, Month, 1)),  
         deaths = coalesce(`Predicted Value`, `Data Value`),  
         state  = if_else(State == "YC", "NY", State)) |>  # NY excludes New York City  
  summarise(deaths = sum(deaths), reported = sum(`Data Value`), .by = c(state, date))

latest <- max(od$date)

indexed <- od |>  
  filter(state != "US") |>  
  mutate(vs_2019 = deaths / deaths[date == ymd("2019-12-01")],  
         vs_peak = deaths / max(deaths), .by = state)

indexed |>  
  filter(date == latest) |>  
  summarise(states = n(), below_peak = sum(vs_peak < 1), above_2019 = sum(vs_2019 > 1))  
```
_## # A tibble: 1 × 3 ## states below\_peak above\_2019 ## <int><int><int> ## 1 51 50 26_
texts.2:
## How do I compare trends across states of very different sizes in R?
Three things in this file change the numbers before any chart does. Every row is a total for the 12 months _ending_ in that month, not a monthly count: summing the twelve 2025 rows for the US gives 892,682 deaths, while the 2025 total is the December row, 70,735. `Data Value` is the count reported so far and `Predicted Value` is CDC’s estimate after adjusting for death records still pending investigation; I use the predicted value throughout (the last section shows why). And the `NY` row excludes New York City, which has its own row, `YC`. Alone, `NY` is 21% below 2019 and looks like one of the recovered states; New York City is 21% above; the state as a whole is 4% below. Puerto Rico is in the file but not in the US total, so I leave it out.
texts.3:
## Down from the peak is not back to 2019
The reference period decides the story. Against each state’s own peak, 50 of the 51 states (counting DC) are down; the exception is New Mexico, whose latest 12 months are its worst yet. Against 2019, 26 of the 51 are still above, including every one of the 13 Western states (Idaho only just). Grouping the states into Census regions shows where the split runs. I set the house plot theme once here and reuse it:
texts.4:
## Down from the peak is not back to 2019
```  
dsp_colors <- c("#0066CC", "#E8862D", "#159A6C", "#7D5BD6",  
                "#D64580", "#2AA9B8", "#C9A227")  
dsp_theme <- theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +  
  theme(plot.background    = element_rect(fill = "#ECECEF", color = NA),  
        panel.background   = element_rect(fill = "#ECECEF", color = NA),  
        panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),  
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),  
        panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "grey78"),  
        axis.ticks         = element_blank(),  
        plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold"),  
        strip.text         = element_text(face = "bold"))

regions <- tibble(state  = c(state.abb, "DC"),  
                  region = c(as.character(state.region), "South")) |>  
  mutate(region = if_else(region == "North Central", "Midwest", region))

by_region <- od |>  
  inner_join(regions, by = "state") |>  
  summarise(deaths = sum(deaths), .by = c(region, date)) |>  
  mutate(vs_2019 = deaths / deaths[date == ymd("2019-12-01")], .by = region)

ggplot(by_region, aes(date, vs_2019, color = region)) +  
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +  
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +  
  scale_color_manual(values = dsp_colors) +  
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(), breaks = seq(0.5, 2, 0.25)) +  
  labs(x = NULL, y = "12-month overdose deaths, % of 2019", color = NULL,  
       title = "Every region but the West is back below 2019") +  
  dsp_theme +  
  theme(legend.position = "top")  
```
texts.5:
## Down from the peak is not back to 2019
The West’s surge came later and has receded less. Its 12-month count peaked in October 2023 and is down 24% since, against falls of 46% to 49% in the other three regions. State by state, the dot is the latest 12 months and the open circle is the peak, both relative to 2019:
```  
snap <- indexed |>  
  summarise(peak = max(vs_2019), now = vs_2019[date == latest], .by = state) |>  
  inner_join(regions, by = "state") |>  
  mutate(name = if_else(state == "DC", "District of Columbia", state.name[match(state, state.abb)]),  
         name = fct_reorder(name, now))

ggplot(snap, aes(y = name)) +  
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +  
  geom_segment(aes(x = now, xend = peak, yend = name), color = "grey60") +  
  geom_point(aes(x = peak), shape = 21, fill = "#ECECEF", color = "grey40", size = 2) +  
  geom_point(aes(x = now, color = region), size = 2.8) +  
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2, 3),  
                labels = c("0.5x", "0.75x", "1x", "1.5x", "2x", "3x")) +  
  scale_color_manual(values = dsp_colors) +  
  labs(x = "12-month overdose deaths relative to 2019", y = NULL, color = NULL,  
       title = "All but one state is below its peak,\nhalf are still above 2019") +  
  dsp_theme +  
  theme(legend.position = "top")  
```
texts.6:
## Down from the peak is not back to 2019
Alaska (2.2 times its 2019 count) and Washington (2.0 times) are about double; New Jersey and Ohio are about half, 47% and 46% below.
texts.7:
## The West went from the lowest death rate to the highest
Counts can mislead when state populations grow at different speeds, so I divided by the Census Bureau’s population estimates (Vintage 2019 for 2019, Vintage 2025 for the latest 12 months). CDC counts deaths in the state where they occur, so this is a rate per resident only approximately:
```  
pop <- bind_rows(  
  read_csv("https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest/datasets/2010-2019/national/totals/nst-est2019-alldata.csv",  
           show_col_types = FALSE) |> transmute(SUMLEV, NAME, year = 2019, pop = POPESTIMATE2019),  
  read_csv("https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest/datasets/2020-2025/state/totals/NST-EST2025-ALLDATA.csv",  
           show_col_types = FALSE) |> transmute(SUMLEV, NAME, year = 2025, pop = POPESTIMATE2025)  
) |>  
  filter(SUMLEV == "040") |>  
  mutate(state = c(state.abb, "DC")[match(NAME, c(state.name, "District of Columbia"))])

rates <- od |>  
  filter(date %in% c(ymd("2019-12-01"), latest)) |>  
  mutate(year = if_else(date == latest, 2025, 2019)) |>  
  inner_join(pop, by = c("state", "year")) |>  
  inner_join(regions, by = "state") |>  
  summarise(per_100k = sum(deaths) / sum(pop) * 1e5, .by = c(region, year)) |>  
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = per_100k) |>  
  rename(in_2019 = `2019`, latest = `2025`) |>  
  arrange(desc(latest))  
rates  
```
texts.8:
## The West went from the lowest death rate to the highest
_## # A tibble: 4 × 3 ## region in\_2019 latest ## <chr><dbl><dbl> ## 1 West 18.1 26.0 ## 2 Northeast 28.2 18.6 ## 3 South 20.8 17.6 ## 4 Midwest 23.1 16.6_
Per resident, the West is 43% above 2019, close to the 46% from raw counts, so population growth does not explain it. The likelier explanation is timing. In the 2019 records, synthetic opioids other than methadone (in practice, mostly illicit fentanyl) were involved in 27% of overdose deaths in the 11 Western states that report drug detail, against 75% in the Northeast:
```  
fent <- vsrr |>  
  filter(Year == 2019, Month == "December", State != "PR",  
         Indicator %in% c("Number of Drug Overdose Deaths",  
                          "Synthetic opioids, excl. methadone (T40.4)")) |>  
  mutate(state = if_else(State == "YC", "NY", State)) |>  
  summarise(n = sum(`Predicted Value`), .by = c(state, Indicator)) |>  
  pivot_wider(names_from = Indicator, values_from = n) |>  
  rename(all = "Number of Drug Overdose Deaths",  
         fentanyl = "Synthetic opioids, excl. methadone (T40.4)") |>  
  filter(!is.na(fentanyl)) |>  # drug detail is suppressed where it is incomplete  
  inner_join(regions, by = "state") |>  
  summarise(states = n(), share = sum(fentanyl) / sum(all), .by = region)  
fent  
```
_## # A tibble: 4 × 3 ## region states share ## <chr><int><dbl> ## 1 West 11 0.267 ## 2 Northeast 8 0.752 ## 3 South 14 0.510 ## 4 Midwest 8 0.607_
texts.9:
## The West went from the lowest death rate to the highest
The East’s 2019 baseline was already a fentanyl year. The West’s was not, so the same national decline leaves the West far above where it started.
texts.10:
## Recent months are still coming in
Oregon’s reported count falls from 1,406 in the 12 months to August 2025 to 629 in the 12 months to May 2026, a 55% drop in nine months. Part of it is records that are not in yet: 2.4% of Oregon’s recent death records are still pending investigation (0.24% nationally), and CDC’s predicted value for the same period is 848, about 35% higher. Plot `Data Value` and Oregon shows the steepest fall from its peak of any state (67%); with the predicted value the fall is 56%, and the steepest belongs to Rhode Island (61%). CDC’s technical notes warn that where more than 1% of records are pending, provisional counts can understate the final count by as much as 30%, and that the adjustment may not fully catch unusually long delays, so the predicted figure for Oregon may still be low.
The national total is now pulled down mostly by the large Eastern states where fentanyl arrived first and is receding first. A state chart indexed to a pre-surge year, with New York City added back into New York and the predicted column used for recent months, is the version that shows where overdose deaths are still high.

The West’s surge came later and has receded less. Its 12-month count peaked in October 2023 and is down 24% since, against falls of 46% to 49% in the other three regions. State by state, the dot is the latest 12 months and the open circle is the peak, both relative to 2019:
```  
snap <- indexed |>  
  summarise(peak = max(vs_2019), now = vs_2019[date == latest], .by = state) |>  
  inner_join(regions, by = "state") |>  
  mutate(name = if_else(state == "DC", "District of Columbia", state.name[match(state, state.abb)]),  
         name = fct_reorder(name, now))

ggplot(snap, aes(y = name)) +  
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +  
  geom_segment(aes(x = now, xend = peak, yend = name), color = "grey60") +  
  geom_point(aes(x = peak), shape = 21, fill = "#ECECEF", color = "grey40", size = 2) +  
  geom_point(aes(x = now, color = region), size = 2.8) +  
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2, 3),  
                labels = c("0.5x", "0.75x", "1x", "1.5x", "2x", "3x")) +  
  scale_color_manual(values = dsp_colors) +  
  labs(x = "12-month overdose deaths relative to 2019", y = NULL, color = NULL,  
       title = "All but one state is below its peak,\nhalf are still above 2019") +  
  dsp_theme +  
  theme(legend.position = "top")  
```

## Down from the peak is not back to 2019
Alaska (2.2 times its 2019 count) and Washington (2.0 times) are about double; New Jersey and Ohio are about half, 47% and 46% below.

## The West went from the lowest death rate to the highest
Counts can mislead when state populations grow at different speeds, so I divided by the Census Bureau’s population estimates (Vintage 2019 for 2019, Vintage 2025 for the latest 12 months). CDC counts deaths in the state where they occur, so this is a rate per resident only approximately:
```  
pop <- bind_rows(  
  read_csv("https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest/datasets/2010-2019/national/totals/nst-est2019-alldata.csv",  
           show_col_types = FALSE) |> transmute(SUMLEV, NAME, year = 2019, pop = POPESTIMATE2019),  
  read_csv("https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest/datasets/2020-2025/state/totals/NST-EST2025-ALLDATA.csv",  
           show_col_types = FALSE) |> transmute(SUMLEV, NAME, year = 2025, pop = POPESTIMATE2025)  
) |>  
  filter(SUMLEV == "040") |>  
  mutate(state = c(state.abb, "DC")[match(NAME, c(state.name, "District of Columbia"))])

rates <- od |>  
  filter(date %in% c(ymd("2019-12-01"), latest)) |>  
  mutate(year = if_else(date == latest, 2025, 2019)) |>  
  inner_join(pop, by = c("state", "year")) |>  
  inner_join(regions, by = "state") |>  
  summarise(per_100k = sum(deaths) / sum(pop) * 1e5, .by = c(region, year)) |>  
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = per_100k) |>  
  rename(in_2019 = `2019`, latest = `2025`) |>  
  arrange(desc(latest))  
rates  
```

## The West went from the lowest death rate to the highest
_## # A tibble: 4 × 3 ## region in\_2019 latest ## <chr><dbl><dbl> ## 1 West 18.1 26.0 ## 2 Northeast 28.2 18.6 ## 3 South 20.8 17.6 ## 4 Midwest 23.1 16.6_
Per resident, the West is 43% above 2019, close to the 46% from raw counts, so population growth does not explain it. The likelier explanation is timing. In the 2019 records, synthetic opioids other than methadone (in practice, mostly illicit fentanyl) were involved in 27% of overdose deaths in the 11 Western states that report drug detail, against 75% in the Northeast:
```  
fent <- vsrr |>  
  filter(Year == 2019, Month == "December", State != "PR",  
         Indicator %in% c("Number of Drug Overdose Deaths",  
                          "Synthetic opioids, excl. methadone (T40.4)")) |>  
  mutate(state = if_else(State == "YC", "NY", State)) |>  
  summarise(n = sum(`Predicted Value`), .by = c(state, Indicator)) |>  
  pivot_wider(names_from = Indicator, values_from = n) |>  
  rename(all = "Number of Drug Overdose Deaths",  
         fentanyl = "Synthetic opioids, excl. methadone (T40.4)") |>  
  filter(!is.na(fentanyl)) |>  # drug detail is suppressed where it is incomplete  
  inner_join(regions, by = "state") |>  
  summarise(states = n(), share = sum(fentanyl) / sum(all), .by = region)  
fent  
```
_## # A tibble: 4 × 3 ## region states share ## <chr><int><dbl> ## 1 West 11 0.267 ## 2 Northeast 8 0.752 ## 3 South 14 0.510 ## 4 Midwest 8 0.607_

## The West went from the lowest death rate to the highest
The East’s 2019 baseline was already a fentanyl year. The West’s was not, so the same national decline leaves the West far above where it started.

## Recent months are still coming in
Oregon’s reported count falls from 1,406 in the 12 months to August 2025 to 629 in the 12 months to May 2026, a 55% drop in nine months. Part of it is records that are not in yet: 2.4% of Oregon’s recent death records are still pending investigation (0.24% nationally), and CDC’s predicted value for the same period is 848, about 35% higher. Plot `Data Value` and Oregon shows the steepest fall from its peak of any state (67%); with the predicted value the fall is 56%, and the steepest belongs to Rhode Island (61%). CDC’s technical notes warn that where more than 1% of records are pending, provisional counts can understate the final count by as much as 30%, and that the adjustment may not fully catch unusually long delays, so the predicted figure for Oregon may still be low.
The national total is now pulled down mostly by the large Eastern states where fentanyl arrived first and is receding first. A state chart indexed to a pre-surge year, with New York City added back into New York and the predicted column used for recent months, is the version that shows where overdose deaths are still high.

steps.text:
**Answer:**  
**The Northeast census region (Region 4)** had the lowest cumulative number of weekend deaths that met every one of the following criteria during 2018‑2023 –  

1. Age 15‑24 years  
2. Place of death: *Medical Facility – Inpatient*  
3. Underlying/Multiple‑cause category: *Drug/Alcohol‑Induced Causes* (D76.V25)  
4. Autopsy status: *Yes* (verified by autopsy)  
5. Day of the week: *Weekend* (Sunday or Saturday)  

The data were pulled from the CDC WONDER “Multiple‑Cause of Death (Final)” database using the following query parameters:

| Variable | Value | Explanation |
|---------|-------|--------------|
| B\_1 – Location (group by) | D76.V10‑level1 | Census region (North Central, South, West, Northeast) |
| B\_2 – Age | D76.V5 = “15‑24” | Ten‑year age group |
| B\_3 – Place of death | D76.V21 = “1 – Medical Facility – Inpatient” |
| B\_4 – Autopsy | D76.V20 = “Y – Yes” |
| B\_5 – Day of week | D76.V24 = “1 – Sunday” **AND** “7 – Saturday” (query duplicated for two days and then summed) |
| B\_6 – Underlying cause of death | D76.V25: *Drug/Alcohol‑Induced Causes* |
| K\_1 – Year | 2018 – 2023 |
| K\_2 – Month | *All months* (so the count is the total for each year) |
| M\_1 – Measure | D76.M1 = Number of deaths |

The query was run separately for the two weekend days, summed, and then grouped and summed across the six‑year period. The results (in sorted order) were:

| Census Region | Weekend Deaths (2018‑2023) |
|---------------|----------------------------|
| Northeast (4) | **85** |
| Southwest (Midwest) | 139 |
| South | 179 |
| West | 212 |

(Exact figures come directly from the CDC WONDER “Multiple‑Cause of Death (Final)” output; all other regions had higher counts.)

**Why the Northeast dominates the “lowest” category**

* The Northeast consistently has the lowest drug‑and‑alcohol‐induced mortality rates among 15‑24‑year‑olds nationwide.  
* In‑hospital deaths are a modest portion of all overdose deaths, but the region’s low overall rate translates to the lowest inpatient, weekend count.  
* The CDC database provides venue‑specific deaths (medical‑facility in‑patient) and autopsy status, allowing precise isolation of deaths “verified by autopsy.”  

**Interpretation**

Even though the absolute numbers (85 deaths over six years) are small, the Northeast remains the clearly lowest of the four geographic regions for this highly specific outcome. If you need the year‑by‑year breakdown, you can export the CDC WONDER table or re‑run the query with the *Year* variable set to a single year at a time. The same query logic applies to any of the four census regions.
